hints: Look closely at what is being injected: ready-made antibodies, not rabies antigen or vaccine. Ask yourself, did the patient make these antibodies themselves?
Remember the rule for passive immunity: if there is no antigen exposure, there is no activation of B cells and no memory cells formed, so what will happen to those foreign proteins over time?
walkthrough:
**Identify the type of immunity**

This is a lovely, classic immunity-type question. The patient is given ready-made antibodies, so they did not make them. That is passive immunity.

Because it is given by injection in a clinic, it is artificial, not natural. Natural passive would be like antibodies across the placenta or in breast milk. So statement 1 is false.

**What happens to injected antibodies?**

Antibodies are proteins, and like all proteins in the body they do not last forever. They will be broken down by enzymes and removed.

The patient is not making replacements because their own B cells were never activated. So statement 2 is true.

**Why is there no memory and only short protection?**

Memory cells only form when your own immune system meets antigen and goes through selection and clonal expansion. Here there was no antigen, only antibody, so no memory cells are made.

That means statement 3 is false, and because the donated antibodies are soon broken down, protection fades quickly. So statement 4 is true. Together, 2 and 4 point to D.

options.A: Incorrect because both 1 and 3 are false. It is artificial, not natural, passive immunity and no memory cells are formed.
options.B: Incorrect because 1 is false. The immunity is artificial passive (injected), not natural passive, even though 4 is true.
options.C: Incorrect because 3 is false. Without antigen there is no B cell activation, so no memory cells to respond faster next time, even though 2 is true.
options.D: Correct because 2 and 4 are true. Injected antibodies are broken down as proteins and not replaced, so protection is immediate but only short-lived.
